title: Five steps
hookLine: psychologist Everett Worthington's REACH model: recall, empathize, give the gift, commit, hold on

cards: A psychologist spends his working life studying forgiveness. He builds a method, teaches it in workshops, writes it up in books. Then life tests the method on him.

Everett Worthington has written that after his mother was killed in a break-in at her home, he found himself walking through his own steps, one by one, to see whether they would hold for the person who had built them.
They weren't a theory anymore. The method's name is five letters, R, E, A, C, H, and each letter is a step.

teach.b: R is recall: remember the hurt as plainly as you can, without turning the other person into a monster or yourself into nothing but a victim. Just what happened.

teach.h: E: SEE THEM FROM THE INSIDE.
teach.b: E is empathize: try to see the one who hurt you from the inside. What fear, pressure or story might they have been carrying that day? This step has old company.

Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor, wrote in his private notebook, in George Long's translation: "When a man has done thee any wrong, immediately consider with what opinion about good or evil he has done wrong."
The emperor and the psychologist point the same way: understanding comes before letting go. And understanding is not agreeing. A is the altruistic gift.

teach.h: A, C: A GIFT, THEN A COMMITMENT.
teach.b: Worthington asks people to remember a time they themselves were forgiven, then offer forgiveness the way a gift is offered, freely, not because it was earned.
C is commit: say it to a friend, or write it down, so the decision has a shape outside your head.

teach.h: H: HOLD ON WHEN IT COMES BACK.
teach.b: H is hold on. The hurt can come back, and in Worthington's telling that isn't proof the forgiveness failed.

teach.h: CONSIDER WITH WHAT OPINION HE HAS DONE WRONG.
teach.b: It's a moment to return to what you decided. You don't have to climb all five at once. A person can stand on recall a long while, or find empathy the steepest stair.
It's a staircase, not an exam, and any single stair is a real place to stand.

how: Psychologists who use Everett Worthington's REACH model usually teach it in groups or workbooks, taking people through recall, empathy, the gift of forgiveness, a commitment and holding on, one step at a time.

o: REACH: Worthington's five stairs toward forgiving
five rules for making a sincere apology, in order
the five stages of grief, from denial to acceptance

games.q: five letters, five steps — tap the pairs.
p: say it aloud or write it down

s: REACH asks you to finish all five steps at once
it's a staircase. any one step is a real place to stand.
in REACH, empathy means agreeing with what they did
understanding is not agreeing. you try to see what they were carrying, not to approve it.
Marcus Aurelius told himself to consider the wrongdoer's opinion of good and evil
"immediately consider with what opinion about good or evil he has done wrong."

games.q: a week after you decided to forgive, the old hurt flares up again. in Worthington's model, what does that mean?
o: the forgiveness failed, so start again from nothing.
it's the last step: hold on to what you decided.
it's a sign to go and confront them.
games.why: H is hold on. in Worthington's telling, a returning hurt isn't proof the forgiveness failed. it's the moment to go back to what you decided.

practice: Choose one modest hurt and one step only: for recall, tell yourself what happened in two plain sentences with no villain in them; for empathy, ask what that person might have been carrying that day; for the gift, remember one time someone let you off.
Stay with that single step while the breath comes and goes; the top of the staircase can wait.

wordCard.voice: Five steps. Recall, empathize, give the gift, commit, hold on: Everett Worthington's REACH, a staircase you can climb one stair at a time. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: one step. One stair is still a stair. Nine hundred sixty-seven days now.

sources.ref: the REACH model (recall, empathize, altruistic gift, commit, hold on)
